summary: Rocky Mountain NP lookout built 1914 on Twin Sisters; replacement and removal dates conflict across sources; the 1914 stone shelter still stands as a radio repeater.

facts.design: Stone crew shelter built 1914; lookout first a small white wood cab, later steel towers
facts.status_note: The lookout tower is gone; the 1914 stone shelter still stands and is used as a radio repeater station

events.note: Originally built by the U.S. Forest Service; the stone shelter is dated to the same year
H.G. Knowles, a fire guard from Longmont, assigned to take charge of the station (July 1914 announcement of the plan)
Trail up the mountain reported completed in the September 18, 1914 item
Fire Observer Heaton in charge (July 1917 item)
Windy Gulch Trail fire seen from the lookout and checked by rangers (August 1922)
National Park Service took over operation of the station
New $16,000 lookout reported completed June 1950; FFLOS says replaced 1950; NRHP nomination says the replacement was built 1949
Destroyed by high winds per FFLOS; a March 1951 newspaper report says the station had fallen
FFLOS: replaced with an L4-cabbed steel tower
NRHP nomination: lookout abandoned and removed in 1969
Stone shelter converted to a fire cache and radio repeater station
Wikipedia: dismantled and removed in 1977 by Youth Conservation Corps members (disputed)
Stone building added to the National Register of Historic Places

resolved_conflicts.explanation: FFLOS says replaced in 1950, wind-destroyed in 1951 and replaced again in 1953. Newspapers confirm a 1950 completion and a 1951 collapse. The NRHP nomination says a replacement built in 1949 stayed active until 1969. Wikipedia says a steel building replaced it in 1950. The story reports the disagreement rather than choosing.

FFLOS says the last steel tower was taken down in 1976; the NRHP nomination says the lookout was abandoned and removed in 1969; Wikipedia says it was dismantled in 1977. The story gives the spread of dates.

notes_for_editor: Four sources disagree on the replacement and removal years (1949, 1950, 1953; 1969, 1976, 1977); the story reports the spread. The NRHP nomination is a PDF with later amendments. The 1914 stone building is the one structure that still stands; no source read describes visitor access to it, so no access fact is recorded. Photos cited on the FFLOS page were not fetched as images, so none were added.
